prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat electronic bands in twisted bilayer graphene at a magic angle and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in moire flat bands

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is one of the few cases in which a calculation anticipated a qualitatively new electronic regime and experiment then delivered it. The Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model (2011) predicted that a single geometric parameter, the twist angle, flattens the bands; the 2018 Jarillo-Herrero experiments found correlated insulators and superconductivity at that angle. Within a few years many independent groups reproduced the phenomena and extended them to other moire systems, including twisted TMDs and fractional Chern insulators. The prediction-then-confirmation structure, the breadth of follow-on physics (correlation, topology, magnetism) and the tunability of the platform make this the strongest case on the shortlist for a discovery that nature supplied. Seven of eight members ranked it, and five placed it in their top three.
statement.case_against: The credited names leave out people whose contributions may be decisive: Yuan Cao as first author of the 2018 experiments, Cory Dean and others for the related moire work, and earlier theory on twisted-bilayer band structure (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto). The three-person limit makes a fully fair allocation impossible. The microscopic origin of the superconductivity is also unresolved, and Mehlig and Olsson have said recognition might still be early. A committee could reasonably conclude that the field is still moving and that a more settled achievement, the clocks or topological insulators, is the safer choice this year.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B013 first as a theory-plus-experiment prize, with the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction and the Jarillo-Herrero experiments as the decisive contributions, and notes that the credit list leaves out other experimental groups.
responses.response: I agree on the structure and on the maturity: the existence of the flat-band platform is secure even though the pairing mechanism is not, so the open mechanism question does not undermine the discovery. I differ slightly on how much the omissions matter. I think they cannot be repaired within a three-name cap, and the committee should say so openly in the citation rather than treat the list as complete. I would still keep Bistritzer, because the prediction is his and MacDonald's jointly.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B008 (Aharonov-Bohm and Berry phases) first, ranks B013 third, and warns that moire recognition may be somewhat early because the superconductivity mechanism and the correlated states are still debated.
responses.response: I take the timing concern seriously but weigh it differently. What the prize would reward is the flat-band prediction and the observation of the correlated phases, both reproduced many times, not an explanation of pairing. Eight years is also not short compared with other recent condensed-matter prizes. On B008 I accept the conceptual weight, since geometric phases underlie topological band theory, which I use every day. But Aharonov-Bohm (1959) and Berry (1984) are two separate discoveries, and a joint citation honours a lineage rather than one result. It also overlaps with the 2016 topological prize. I would keep B008 off my list for that reason.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the optical lattice clock (B061) first, calling it a clean, concrete advance whose atomic physics she can judge directly. She ranks B013 second and says that the omission of Cao and others complicates fairness.
responses.response: B061 is the strongest alternative and I put it in second place. Its two-name credit is cleaner than B013's and its confirmation is more complete. My reservation is about the type of discovery. The clock is a superb invention and measurement advance, whereas twisted bilayer graphene opened a new physical regime. I share your concern about the credit gaps in B013, but that is a drawback of the list rather than a weakness of the physics. If the committee prefers fairness of attribution to breadth of impact, I would move to B061 without much resistance.

responses.point: Johansson ranks Cirac-Zoller (B034) first, as the conceptual blueprint for ion and cold-atom quantum information processing. He ranks B013 second and flags that Yuan Cao is not credited.
responses.response: The Cirac-Zoller proposals are original and have been confirmed thoroughly, and I do not doubt their quality. My difficulty is that the experimental realisations that made them real (Wineland and Blatt, partly recognised in 2012) are largely outside the credited pair, so we would honour the blueprint without the demonstrations. The B013 case has theory and experiment together in one coherent set. On Cao, we agree that this is a real gap, but the shortlist offers no way to credit him.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can accept an incomplete credit set for B013 (Cao, Dean, and earlier twisted-bilayer theory are not among the credited names), or would prefer the cleaner B061 allocation.
Whether the unresolved mechanism of superconductivity in magic-angle graphene makes recognition premature for some members.
I rely on my own recollection of the chronology and have not verified it independently.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile. My own research in electronic structure and magnetism is adjacent to moire flat-band physics, but I have no documented collaboration or institutional tie with any of the credited candidates.
